analysis.one_liner: Gives struggling homeowners facing foreclosure on risky mortgages up to nine months to catch up, and warns borrowers before their rates reset.
analysis.headline: The foreclosure-deferral bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on December 11, 2008, got no further action, and died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act to let eligible homeowners — those with pre-2008 subprime or negative-amortization mortgages who live in the home and earn under 200% of area median income — legally defer foreclosure for up to 270 days. During that time they would pay a reduced monthly amount (roughly their original payment, with the difference added back over the loan's life), and servicers could not charge late fees. Servicers would also have to warn borrowers in writing 120 days before a rate reset or payment increase, listing options like refinancing and counseling. It was introduced in the Senate on December 11, 2008, referred to the Banking Committee, and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners with subprime or negative-amortization mortgages taken out before 2008 who faced foreclosure after a rate reset or payment jump, and who lived in the home and earned under 200% of area median income, would gain up to nine months of protection from losing their home — paying the lower original payment during the deferment, with no late fees, plus advance written warning of coming payment increases. Housing counseling groups would also gain from a $200 million funding authorization.

how_it_helps.text: Homeowners with subprime or negative-amortization loans could stop any foreclosure — including a foreclosure sale — for up to 270 days by notifying their servicer and making reduced monthly payments.

During the deferment period, the monthly payment would drop to roughly the original loan payment (or, for negative-amortization loans, the original minimum payment), with the difference added back over the life of the loan — so the homeowner gets time to recover income or arrange a modification rather than losing the house.

Servicers would be barred from charging late fees or any other fees during the deferment period, and would have to send clear written warning at least 120 days before any rate reset or payment increase, listing alternatives like refinancing, forbearance, and counseling.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage servicers, lenders, and investors who hold the loans: they would lose up to nine months of full payments and late fees, wait longer to foreclose on delinquent loans, and absorb the difference between the deferment payment and the contract payment as a longer amortizing balance.

drawbacks.text: The deferment delays but does not erase the debt: the difference between the original payment and the reduced deferment payment is added back and amortized over the life of the loan, so borrowers pay it back with interest eventually.

Lenders and mortgage investors would absorb months of reduced payments with no late fees and no ability to foreclose during the period, which could raise the cost or reduce the availability of mortgage credit — a cost honest supporters would acknowledge.

The right was limited to owner-occupants below 200% of area median income with pre-2008 subprime or negative-amortization loans, so it offered nothing to other struggling homeowners and covered only a slice of the foreclosure crisis.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to struggling homeowners — a guaranteed pause in foreclosure and a reset payment they could afford — was substantial, and the cost to lenders was deferrable, not forgiven: missed amounts were spread over the life of the loan, homeowners had to keep making payments and maintain the property, and servicers retained the debt. The honest objection is that giving delinquent borrowers a court-enforceable hold on foreclosure for up to nine months could increase losses for mortgage investors and slow the housing recovery that everyone, including homeowners, depended on. But at the depths of the 2008 crisis, the direct benefit to families at risk of losing their homes outweighed that cost, and the bill never received even a committee hearing to test that trade-off.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Menendez introduced the bill on December 11, 2008, in the final weeks of the 110th Congress, amid the worst housing and financial crisis since the Depression.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day; that was the only action the bill ever received.
The committee never took it up, and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, without the bill receiving any vote — the standard end for a bill that dies in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage servicers and loan holders avoided a statutory pause on foreclosures; homeowners in foreclosure got no federal deferral right from this bill.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Banking Committee; no further action.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 11, 2008, and never held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it out.

against.name: Mortgage servicing and financial industry
against.role: Mortgage servicers, lenders, and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: The financial industry broadly opposed government intervention in foreclosures during the crisis; industry pressure was widely reported as a factor shaping the congressional response to the foreclosure wave.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so no roll-call shows where parties stood; it had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and died in a Democratic-controlled Senate committee.

industries.note: The bill would have forced servicers to delay foreclosures on delinquent subprime and payment-shock loans for up to nine months while the borrower paid only the original (lower) payment, with no late fees — costing servicers and loan holders payments and foreclosure proceeds during the crisis. Their interest ran against homeowners trying to keep their homes.

industries.industry: Housing counseling organizations (Neighborhood Reinvestment Corporation and HUD-approved counselors)
industries.note: The bill authorized $200 million for foreclosure mitigation counseling — more counselors, translators, and outreach to help homeowners navigate foreclosure. These services help homeowners directly.
